n: Amos was not a professional prophet but a herdsman from Tekoa, a village south of Bethlehem in Judah. He was sent north to preach to Israel around 760 BC, a time of prosperity under King Jeroboam II.

f.g: A village about 10 miles (16 km) south of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness.

n: Amos’s theme sentence: the Lord roars like a lion from Jerusalem. Even the green pastures and fertile Mount Carmel wither at His voice. Amos, a shepherd, knew what a lion’s roar meant.

f.w: The LORD will roar from Zion

f.g: A lush, wooded ridge on Israel’s northern coast; if Carmel dries up, everything does.

n: Amos begins with Israel’s enemies. “Three transgressions, and for four” is a Hebrew way of saying “sin upon sin, more than enough.” Damascus (Syria) brutally crushed the Israelite region of Gilead.

f.g: A numeric pattern (x, x+1) meaning the sins have piled up past the limit.

n: Fire will consume the royal houses of Syria. Hazael and Ben-hadad were Syrian kings who had attacked Israel.

f.g: A name or title used by several kings of Damascus.

n: The gates of Damascus will be broken and its people exiled to Kir. This came true when Assyria conquered Damascus in 732 BC.

f.g: The heavy beam that locked the city gate.
“Valley of wickedness” — probably a wordplay on a place name.

n: Gaza, a Philistine city, captured whole communities and sold them as slaves to Edom. Trafficking in human beings is condemned.

f.g: A Philistine city on the southern coast.

n: The same fire of judgment will burn Gaza’s walls and palaces.

f.g: A refrain repeated for each nation, stressing that God’s justice is consistent.

n: The other Philistine cities — Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron — will also fall. God’s judgment reaches the whole Philistine league.

f.g: In KJV, “GOD” in capitals represents the divine name YHWH (Jehovah).

n: Tyre also sold captives to Edom, breaking a “brotherly covenant” — perhaps the old treaty of friendship between Hiram of Tyre and David and Solomon.

f.g: Tyre, the great Phoenician port city.

n: Tyre’s strong island walls will not save it from God’s fire.
Edom, descended from Esau, kept attacking Israel, his “brother” Jacob’s descendants, with relentless hatred. Unforgiving anger is a sin God judges.

f.g: Literally “destroyed his compassions” — smothered all natural family feeling.

n: Teman and Bozrah, Edom’s major cities, will burn.

f.g: A region or city in Edom, known for its wise men.

n: The Ammonites committed horrific war crimes against pregnant women just to grab more land. Amos insists God holds even foreign nations accountable for cruelty.

f.g: A people east of the Jordan, descended from Lot.

n: Rabbah, Ammon’s capital (modern Amman, Jordan), will be destroyed amid battle cries and storm.

f.g: A violent storm — a picture of God’s overwhelming power.

n: Ammon’s king and his officials will be carried away together into exile.

f.g: Hebrew malkam; some see a wordplay on Milcom, Ammon’s god.
